## Overview

The Archi people (Archi: аршишттиб, arshishttib) are a Lezgic ethnic group living in eight villages in southern Dagestan, Russia. Archib is their “parent village,” where the whole community formerly reassembled for three months each year to undertake communal work. Their habitat lies about 2,000 meters above sea level in the Kara-Koisu basin in the Caucasus. The Archi have a total population of about 1,200 and speak their own language. Their culture is described as one of the most distinct and best-preserved cultures of Dagestan. Their language is a Northeast Caucasian language of the Lezgic branch, while their culture has been described in relation to Avar and Lak culture.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Archi language source records an Archi legend about the origin of the language. In the story, God created nations and peoples, but there were fewer languages than peoples. Several peoples refused to accept the most difficult language in the world, which consequently became the language of the least numerous people in the world: the Archi language and the Archi people. The Archi people article also refers to the first information about the Archi language as a letter from Peter von Uslar to Franz Anton Schiefner, dated June 11, 1863, which included an Archi legend.

## Language & religion

Archi is a Northeast Caucasian language of the Lezgic branch, spoken by the Archis in Archib and the six surrounding smaller villages in southern Dagestan, Russia. It is colloquial, unwritten, and spoken only in several villages; Avar and Lak are widely spoken. The classification of Archi has not been definitively established: it has been treated in relation to Avar, Lak, and the Lezgian–Samur group. The language has four noun classes, an ergative–absolutive structure, and a highly complex phonological system. Until recently it had no written form except in specialist studies using the Latin script. In 2006, the Surrey Morphology Group developed a Cyrillic alphabet based on the Avar alphabet. The Archi are overwhelmingly Sunni Muslims. Arabic monuments in the Kufic script suggest conversion to Islam not later than the 10th century.
